picks.title: Devon Hase: Like the River Flows: Anattā, Impermanence, and the Freedom of no Fixed Address
picks.summary: (Insight Meditation Society - Retreat Center) A dharma talk exploring anattā through the five aggregates and the Anattālakkhaṇa Sutta, alongside Anāthapiṇḍika's deathbed teaching from Sāriputta. Weaves impermanence and death contemplation together with not-self - drawing on Thanissaro Bhikkhu's pragmatic (not metaphysical) framing of not-self - and closes with mettā as the natural fruit of a loosened, undefended heart.
picks.reason: Dharma talk deeply exploring not-self, impermanence, and death contemplation with Buddhist sutta references.

picks.summary: Celebrating Sylvia Boorstein’s 90th birthday, Jack and Sylvia reflect on 49 years of friendship, meditation, and Dharma practice—and how awakening ultimately expresses itself through kindness, connection, and a willingness to stay amazed.Today’s podcast is brought to you by BetterHelp. Give online therapy a try at betterhelp.com/heartwisdom and get on your way to being your best self.This week on Heart Wisdom, Jack Kornfield shares:Sylvia’s journey through the Buddhist teachings of impermanence, suffering, and selflessness, and how intellectual understanding gradually becomes lived realization
picks.reason: Reflection on Buddhist impermanence and kindness through decades of meditation and friendship.

picks.title: 339 – Bright Clarity Appears Before You: Insight When You're "Just Sitting"
picks.summary: When we sit Zazen, even if we're working with a koan, we do not actively try to achieve insight. But nonetheless, Chan and Zen masters throughout history have exhorted us to awaken to Reality. How does insight happen when you're "just sitting?" How do you awaken to what you have not yet seen without getting caught up in concepts of enlightenment and delusion, before and after? How do you lean into the unknown if you're trying to let go of any kind of doing at all?
picks.reason: Insight into how Zen meditation leads to awakening without striving or conceptualizing enlightenment.

picks.title: Nirvana is NOT Nothing | There IS an Unborn, Uncreated, Unconditioned | Nibbana | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: The final goal of Dhamma practice, what it's all about, is to realize Nibbāna (Sanskrit: Nirvāṇa ). It's important to have an accurate understanding of our final objective, otherwise it would be difficult to develop our mind in the right direction. However, as Nibbana / Nirvana is totally beyond all concepts, words, notions and thoughts, even the Buddha can not possibly describe it accurately by means of language. He can only provide similies to inspire us, or he describes what Nibbāna in NOT. For example, the Buddha has stated many times that Nibbana is the end of birth, ageing and death; Nib
picks.reason: Clarifies the Buddhist concept of Nirvana beyond concepts, focusing on what it is not.

picks.title: The Dharma of Chasing Followers
picks.summary: A talk on the dharma of chasing followers: fame, failure, and the fear of being nobody. The wish to be seen, to count, to leave a mark — and what happens when we meet it with awareness instead of feeding it metrics.Recorded at Downtown Dharma DC, August 2026.Texts & references: Khemaka Sutta (SN 22.89) — suttacentral.net/sn22.89 · The dung beetle (SN 17.5) — suttacentral.net/sn17.5 · Iti 26 on giving · D.W. Winnicott on mirroring · Erik Erikson, generativity and integrity
picks.reason: Explores Buddhist texts on self-worth, awareness, and generativity in a dharma talk.

picks.showTitle: Earth Dreams: Zen Buddhism and the Soul of the World
picks.title: All is blessed, all is blessed
picks.summary: Greetings Friends,I am returning from the Grasses, Trees and Great Earth Sesshin at Great Vow Zen Monastery. An outdoor sesshin I have had the deep pleasure of co-leading for the past six years. During the sesshin we practiced various ways of listening to the dharma of the natural world, including:* Hearing with the eyes, heart, whole body. * Letting ourselves be seen by the sky, ferns, rocks and queen ann’s lace. * Becoming tree, black-berry, forest, ground. The great earth and sky speak the dharma through their constancy, reminding us that we too belong to this world, that our presence is me
picks.reason: Zen sesshin reflections on deep listening and connection with nature's dharma.

picks.showTitle: Sounds True: Insights at the Edge
picks.title: [ENCORE EPISODE] Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche: "In Love with the World"
picks.summary: At 36, Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche walked out of his monastery in the middle of the night with a few thousand rupees and no plan. Weeks later, he was dying of food poisoning on a street in India—and chose not to call for help. In this encore episode, Tami Simon speaks with the beloved Tibetan Buddhist teacher about what he found on the other side of that night.Rinpoche is now partnering with Sounds True on a brand-new course, Wild World, Steady Mind: 21 Days to Embrace Modern Reality with Clarity and Calm, filmed on location at his monastery in Nepal. Visit soundstrue.com to learn more.See Privacy
picks.reason: Tibetan Buddhist teacher recounts transformative experience and insight into life.

picks.title: This One Note Is Enough | Chodo Robert Campbell
picks.summary: “We don't have to save everyone, solve everything, or understand the whole mystery of our lives. All we have to do is be in this moment, this breath, this body. Then bow, let go, and listen.”Chodo Sensei shares the story of Kakua, one of the first Japanese monks to travel to China and study Zen. A recluse who preferred remote mountains to monastery fame, Kakua was eventually summoned by the emperor to demonstrate the true teachings he'd acquired. Kakua thought for a moment, reached into the folds of his robe, pulled out a flute, and blew a single note.Then he put the flute away, bowed, and wal
picks.reason: Zen story and teaching emphasizing presence and letting go in this moment.

picks.title: Knowing, Not Interfering | Insight through Awareness | Vipassana | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: To develop insight, vipassana, we have to learn to observe uninterested. We have to be like an objective researcher. We know what we experience, without reacting, interfering and manipulating. We shift our identification towards the 'Knower', rather than the 'Doer'. What we take up as object of our observation, we no longer identify with. We just mindfully know the emotion we're experiencing, we don't have to react to it. It's like watching a movie, and knowing that we're watching a movie. We're not getting sucked into the action, we're aware that we're just looking at images of actors project
picks.reason: Vipassana teaching on observing experience without interference or reaction.

picks.title: How Do You Forgive Someone Who Never Apologizes?
picks.summary: In today’s episode, we explore the deeply personal and transformative practice of forgiveness - and why letting go of resentment is ultimately about changing our own mind rather than waiting for someone else to apologize or make things right.The guest explains how our experience of hurt can become tied to blame, self-blame, and the mistaken belief that our faults or painful experiences define who we are. Drawing on Buddhist teachings and the advice of Venerable Geshe Kelsang Gyatso, including teachings from The New Eight Steps to Happiness, she explores how we can learn to recognize our faults
picks.reason: Explores Buddhist forgiveness practice focusing on changing one's own mind.

picks.title: What Makes SBT Unique
picks.summary: Venerable Tenzin Tarpa is the founder and director of SBT – The Secular Buddhist Tradition. A fully ordained Buddhist monk and student of The Dalai Lama, Venerable Tarpa is a teacher, author, and philosopher with nearly three decades in Buddhist studies, including a decade in Buddhist monasteries in India. SBT – the Secular Buddhist Tradition, is an international spiritual community dedicated to Secular Buddhism and the timeless wisdom of the Buddha. SBT presents the Buddha’s teachings as neither a religion nor exotic belief system, sharing a practical presentation focused on the positive life
picks.reason: Explains the unique approach of Secular Buddhist Tradition and its presentation of Buddha's teachings.
